answers.answer:
Classification context. Both d1uc6a1 and d1o5dt2 sit in SCOPe family b.1.2.1 (fibronectin type III), superfamily b.1.2 (fibronectin type III), fold b.1 (immunoglobulin-like beta-sandwich), class b (all-beta). Family membership is the strong, homology-level statement: both are FNIII domains sharing the seven-strand (A, B, E / C, C', F, G) beta-sandwich core and detectable sequence similarity. Relationship to other b.1 superfamilies (e.g., b.1.1 immunoglobulin) is fold-level only and must not be read as homology. The fragment annotation on d1o5dt2 does not change its classification, because SCOPe assigns the domain by its parent full-length protein, but it changes how much evidence the entry supplies.

What 'fragment' means. SCOPe flags a domain as a fragment when the deposited coordinates cover only part of the domain, typically because the crystallized construct was truncated or because part of the domain is disordered or unmodeled in a large multi-chain complex (1O5D chain T is one chain of a multi-component receptor-type complex; d1o5dt2 is its second region). Before using it, one should confirm from the PDB SEQRES versus ATOM records and remark 465 (missing residues), plus SIFTS/UniProt mapping, which strands are absent and whether the absence is construct design or disorder.

Effect on alignment. (1) Align only over observed residues; treat missing regions as unknown, not as deletions, so gap penalties and identity denominators are computed on the observed length only. (2) Anchor the alignment on the complete domain d1uc6a1 and the FNIII core topology; do not use d1o5dt2 as a profile or HMM seed, because a short partial sequence yields unreliable pairwise identities and could distort the family profile. (3) Structural superposition should report coverage as well as RMSD; a low RMSD over a few strands can look deceptively good.

Effect on representative selection. Complete domains should be preferred as family and superfamily representatives and as template-library entries; d1uc6a1 is the appropriate choice over d1o5dt2. In ASTRAL-style subset construction, fragments should be filtered out (or ranked below complete entries regardless of resolution/SPACI score), because representatives are meant to stand for the whole domain. d1o5dt2 should not be used as the sole homology-modeling template for a full FNIII domain, since missing strands and loops would have to be modeled without structural support.

Effect on interpreting family diversity. A fragment can bias diversity in both directions: partial sequences inflate apparent sequence divergence and can be mistaken for structural variants (e.g., apparent loss of a strand or altered loop), while any real variation in the missing region is invisible. It therefore should not be counted as an independent structural variant in the family, nor used to infer loop-length distributions or binding-surface composition. It remains useful for species/protein-level coverage and for the observed region in its complex context.

Functional limits. FNIII family membership does not transfer function: FNIII modules are generic scaffolds whose ligand sites (e.g., the RGD integrin-binding loop in fibronectin FN10) are not family-wide. For a fragment the limitation is stronger: absent loops mean binding-site residues cannot be inferred at all.
